name: Bhartṛhari
summary: The grammarian-philosopher, author of the Vākyapadīya, its Vṛtti (traditionally) and the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā. He taught that Brahman is the Word-principle appearing as the world, that all cognition is permeated by the word, that meaning is borne by the indivisible sphoṭa and grasped as pratibhā, and that grammar is a door to liberation. The later tradition often identifies him with the poet of the Śatakatraya; the Chinese pilgrim Yijing reports a Bhartṛhari who went back and forth between monastic and household life.

tradition.text: identified by later tradition with the royal poet Bhartṛhari, brother of Vikramāditya (legend)

name: Vasurāta
summary: Named by the commentators as Bhartṛhari's teacher in grammar.
notes: Known only from commentarial report (Puṇyarāja on the closing verses of VP 2, from memory).

name: Vyāḍi
summary: U31 contribution: the ancient grammarian credited with the lost Saṃgraha (said to have had a hundred thousand verses), which Bhartṛhari says declined before Patañjali; in the Mahābhāṣya he holds that a word denotes the individual substance (dravya), against Vājapyāyana's universal.

name: Vājapyāyana
summary: Ancient grammarian cited in Kātyāyana's vārttikas and the Mahābhāṣya (on P 1.2.64) as holding that a word denotes the universal form (ākṛti).

name: Sphoṭāyana
summary: A grammarian named once by Pāṇini (6.1.123); later tradition, reading his name, makes him the originator of the sphoṭa doctrine.
notes: The link with the sphoṭa doctrine is a later traditional inference from the name.

name: Audumbarāyaṇa
summary: An early authority quoted in Yāska's Nirukta (1.1) for the view that speech is 'permanent only in the sense-faculty' (indriya-nitya), read by later grammarians as an early form of the doctrine that the word is grasped as a whole in the mind.

name: Candrācārya
summary: The teacher who, according to the closing verses of the Vākyapadīya's second book, recovered the tradition of the Mahābhāṣya from a mountain region and spread it widely after it had declined.
notes: Some identify him with the Buddhist grammarian Candragomin; the identification is doubtful.

name: Vṛṣabhadeva
summary: Author of the Paddhati, a sub-commentary on the Vṛtti to the first book of the Vākyapadīya.

name: Helārāja
summary: Kashmiri commentator on the third book of the Vākyapadīya (Prakīrṇaprakāśa), who read Bhartṛhari's categories as ways the one Word-Brahman appears; he mentions his own lost commentary Śabdaprabhā and a work Vārttikonmeṣa.

name: Puṇyarāja
summary: Kashmiri commentator to whom the commentary on the second book of the Vākyapadīya is ascribed.

name: Kaiyaṭa
summary: U31 contribution: Kashmiri author of the Pradīpa on the Mahābhāṣya, who reads Patañjali through Bhartṛhari and transmits the sphoṭa doctrine and the Word-monism to the later grammarians.

name: Maṇḍana Miśra
summary: U31 contribution: author of the Sphoṭasiddhi, the classic defence of the sphoṭa against Kumārila; his Brahmasiddhi is sympathetic to the word-brahman.

name: Bharata Miśra
summary: Author of a Sphoṭasiddhi distinct from Maṇḍana's.

name: Ṛṣiputra Parameśvara
summary: Kerala scholar credited with the Gopālikā commentary on Maṇḍana's Sphoṭasiddhi.
notes: Several Kerala scholars named Parameśvara are known; the identification needs checking.

name: Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita
summary: U31 contribution: besides the Siddhāntakaumudī, author of the Vaiyākaraṇa-siddhānta-kārikās, the verse summary of grammatical philosophy that holds, on final analysis, that only the sentence-sphoṭa is real.

name: Kauṇḍa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Nephew of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita and author of the Vaiyākaraṇa-bhūṣaṇa and its abridgment, the Bhūṣaṇa-sāra, which defend the grammarians' theory of meaning and the sphoṭa against Mīmāṃsā and Navya-Nyāya.

name: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa
summary: U31 contribution: the last great classical Pāṇinian philosopher; in the Mañjūṣās and the Sphoṭavāda he systematizes the grammarians' semantics (the three powers of words), identifies the sphoṭa with the madhyamā level of speech, and maps parā, paśyantī, madhyamā and vaikharī onto the root centre, navel, heart and throat.

name: Prabhācandra
summary: Digambara logician, author of the Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa and Nyāyakumudacandra, which refute among other doctrines the grammarians' Word-monism.

name: Bharata (Bharata Muni)
summary: The sage to whom the Nāṭyaśāstra is ascribed: Brahmā taught him the Nāṭyaveda, which he performed with his hundred sons before the gods; his sons' mockery of the sages brought a curse, and drama was brought down to earth at King Nahuṣa's request (NŚ 1, 36).

scholarly.text: the name of the tradition to which the compiled Nāṭyaśāstra is ascribed

realization_account.text: Received the Nāṭyaveda from Brahmā, who composed it by yoga from the four Vedas.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nandikeśvara
summary: U31 contribution: the name under which the Abhinayadarpaṇa (dance and gesture) and other works on dance and music are transmitted; tradition identifies him with Śiva's attendant Nandin, who taught dance.

name: Kohala
summary: Ancient authority on drama, music and dance, named in the Nāṭyaśāstra's list of Bharata's sons and cited by Abhinavagupta and Śārṅgadeva; his works are lost.

name: Bhāmaha
summary: Author of the Kāvyālaṅkāra, the earliest surviving independent treatise on poetics after Bharata; founder of the 'figure' (alaṅkāra) school.

name: Daṇḍin
summary: Author of the Kāvyādarśa; also credited with the prose romance Daśakumāracarita.

name: Vāmana (the poetician)
summary: Author of the Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra, holding that style (rīti) is the soul of poetry; distinct from Vāmana co-author of the Kāśikā.

name: Udbhaṭa
summary: Kashmiri poetician of Jayāpīḍa's court (Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṅgraha); also named as an early commentator on the Nāṭyaśāstra (ŚR 1.1.19).

name: Rudraṭa
summary: Author of a Kāvyālaṅkāra in sixteen chapters, counting ten rasas (with śānta and preyas).

name: Ānandavardhana
summary: Kashmiri poet-theorist, author of the Dhvanyāloka, who established suggestion (dhvani) as the soul of poetry and rasa-dhvani as its highest form; he named śānta the principal rasa of the Mahābhārata.

name: Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa
summary: Early commentator on the Nāṭyaśāstra, known through Abhinavagupta's report: rasa is the stable emotion intensified (upacita) by the determinants, existing primarily in the character (Rāma) and secondarily in the actor who imitates him.
notes: His views are known only through opponents' reports (Abhinavabhāratī, Kāvyaprakāśa).

name: Śrī Śaṅkuka
summary: Commentator on the Nāṭyaśāstra, known through Abhinavagupta's report: rasa is the stable emotion inferred (anumita) in the actor, who is taken as Rāma like a painted horse taken as a horse (citraturaga-nyāya).

name: Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka
summary: Kashmiri theorist (Hṛdayadarpaṇa, lost) who held that rasa is neither produced, inferred nor suggested but 'enjoyed': poetic language 'makes present' (bhāvakatva) the situation in universal form and 'makes it enjoyable' (bhojakatva) in a state of rest in sattva, akin to tasting the supreme Brahman.
notes: Known through Abhinavagupta's and Mahimabhaṭṭa's reports.

name: Bhaṭṭa Tauta
summary: U31 contribution: Abhinavagupta's teacher in dramaturgy, author of the lost Kāvyakautuka.

name: Abhinavagupta
summary: U31 contribution: in the Abhinavabhāratī and the Locana he gave the classical account of rasa — the relish (carvaṇā) of a generalized emotion in the spectator's own consciousness, free of obstacles, at rest in itself (viśrānti), marked by wonder (camatkāra) — and defended śānta as a rasa whose stable basis is knowledge of the self; aesthetic rapture is akin to, not identical with, the bliss of the supreme.

name: Kuntaka
summary: Author of the Vakroktijīvita: striking, oblique expression (vakrokti) is the life of poetry.

name: Mahimabhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Vyaktiviveka, which reduces suggestion to inference.

name: Dhanañjaya
summary: Author of the Daśarūpaka at the court of Muñja of Mālava.

name: Dhanika
summary: Brother of Dhanañjaya and author of the Avaloka commentary on the Daśarūpaka.

name: Bhoja
summary: U31 contribution: King Bhoja of Dhārā, author of the Śṛṅgāraprakāśa and the Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa on poetics, who held that there is one rasa, śṛṅgāra as self-regard (abhimāna).

name: Kṣemendra
summary: Kashmiri polymath, pupil of Abhinavagupta, author of the Aucityavicāracarcā on propriety.

name: Mammaṭa
summary: Kashmiri author of the Kāvyaprakāśa, the most influential synthesis of poetics along the lines of Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta.

name: Ruyyaka
summary: Kashmiri author of the Alaṅkārasarvasva.

name: Viśvanātha Kavirāja
summary: Orissan poet-theorist, author of the Sāhityadarpaṇa, who defined poetry as a sentence whose soul is rasa and called rasa the twin of tasting Brahman.

name: Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja
summary: Telugu-born scholar at the Mughal court (Shāh Jahān) and in Vārāṇasī, author of the Rasagaṅgādhara and devotional poems (Gaṅgālaharī).

name: Rājaśekhara
summary: Poet and dramatist of Kanauj, author of the Kāvyamīmāṃsā.

name: Rāmacandra (Sūri)
summary: Jain monk-poet, disciple of Hemacandra, co-author with Guṇacandra of the Nāṭyadarpaṇa.

name: Guṇacandra
summary: Jain monk, disciple of Hemacandra, co-author of the Nāṭyadarpaṇa.

name: Hemacandra
summary: U31 contribution: author of the Kāvyānuśāsana on poetics and teacher of Rāmacandra and Guṇacandra.

name: Śāradātanaya
summary: Author of the Bhāvaprakāśana.

name: Bhavabhūti
summary: Dramatist of the Uttararāmacarita, Mālatīmādhava and Mahāvīracarita; held that compassion (karuṇa) is the one rasa.

name: Nārada
summary: U31 contribution: the divine sage with the vīṇā, master of gāndharva, to whom the Nāradīya Śikṣā and the Saṅgītamakaranda are ascribed and who is named among the authorities of music (ŚR 1.1.16).

name: Tumburu
summary: The gandharva singer paired with Nārada, named among the authorities of music (ŚR 1.1.16).

name: Dattila
summary: Author of the Dattilam on gāndharva; named among Bharata's sons in the Nāṭyaśāstra and among music's authorities (ŚR 1.1.16).

name: Mataṅga
summary: Author of the Bṛhaddeśī, the first to define rāga, and teacher of the doctrine that the world is made of nāda.

name: Nānyadeva
summary: King of Mithilā (Karṇāṭa dynasty), author of the Bharatabhāṣya.

name: Śārṅgadeva
summary: Author of the Saṅgītaratnākara, of a Kashmiri brahmin family settled at the Yādava court of Devagiri under Siṅghaṇa (ŚR 1.1.2–10); he also wrote a work on the body and self, the Adhyātmaviveka, to which he refers (ŚR 1.2.119).
notes: Wording and locator checked in Phase B against a local e-text in sources_raw/; still a skeleton entry (not fidelity-checked).

name: Kallinātha
summary: Commentator on the Saṅgītaratnākara (Kalānidhi) at the Vijayanagara court.

name: Siṃhabhūpāla
summary: Recherla king and author of the Saṅgītasudhākara commentary on the Saṅgītaratnākara (and of the Rasārṇavasudhākara on dramaturgy).

name: Pārśvadeva
summary: Author of the Saṅgītasamayasāra.

name: Someśvara III
summary: Western Cālukya king, author of the Mānasollāsa (1131 CE).

name: Kumbhakarṇa (Rāṇā Kumbhā)
summary: Mahārāṇā of Mewar, author of the Saṅgītarāja and a commentary on the Gītagovinda.

name: Rāmāmātya
summary: Minister at Vijayanagara, author of the Svaramelakalānidhi.

name: Somanātha (author of the Rāgavibodha)
summary: Author of the Rāgavibodha (1609).

name: Veṅkaṭamakhin
summary: Tanjore scholar, author of the Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā and its seventy-two mela scheme; son of Govinda Dīkṣita.

name: Govinda Dīkṣita
summary: Minister of the Tanjore Nāyakas, to whom the Saṅgītasudhā is ascribed.

name: Ahobala
summary: Author of the Saṅgītapārijāta.

name: Dāmodara (author of the Saṅgītadarpaṇa)
summary: Author of the Saṅgītadarpaṇa.

name: Puṇḍarīka Viṭṭhala
summary: Karnataka-born musicologist at Mughal-era courts of the north, author of the Ṣaḍrāgacandrodaya and other treatises.

name: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar
summary: U31 contribution: one of the three great Karṇāṭaka composers, whose Sanskrit kṛtis are also meditations (the Kamalāmbā Navāvaraṇa kṛtis set the Śrīcakra worship in music); music as worship of the deity through nāda.

name: Śyāma Śāstrī
summary: U31 contribution: eldest of the three great Karṇāṭaka composers, whose songs to the Goddess Kāmākṣī make music a form of devotion.

name: Tyāgarāja
summary: U31 contribution: in his songs on nāda Tyāgarāja teaches that nāda is the body of the Lord and that music joined to devotion (nādopāsanā) is a way to liberation, echoing the Saṅgītaratnākara; one of the three great Karṇāṭaka composers.

name: Purandara Dāsa
summary: U31 contribution: the Haridāsa singer-saint remembered as the 'grandfather' (pitāmaha) of Karṇāṭaka music, who fixed its elementary lessons and made singing the Lord's name the core of practice.

name: Svāmī Haridās
summary: U31 contribution: the Vṛndāvana singer-saint remembered as the master of dhrupad and, by tradition, the teacher of Tānsen.

name: Tānsen
summary: U31 contribution: the court musician of Akbar, remembered as the greatest singer of dhrupad; tradition makes him a pupil of Svāmī Haridās and credits his singing with miraculous effects (lamps lit by Dīpak rāga).

realization_account.text: Stories of lamps lit and rain brought by his rāgas.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Annamācārya
summary: U31 contribution: the Telugu singer-saint of Tirumala whose thousands of saṅkīrtanas to Veṅkaṭeśvara are among the earliest compositions in the pallavi–caraṇa song form.

name: Kṣetrayya
summary: Telugu composer of padams to Muvvagopāla in which the devotee speaks as a woman in love; a basis of the dance repertoire.

name: Svāti Tirunāḷ
summary: Mahārāja of Travancore and composer of devotional songs in several languages and styles.

name: Bodhendra Sarasvatī
summary: Head of the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi maṭha in its own succession list, remembered as a propagator of repeating and singing the divine name (nāma-siddhānta) and as a source of the South Indian bhajana tradition.
notes: Works on the divine name are ascribed to him; titles not recorded here (uncertain).

name: Śrīdhara Ayyāvāḷ
summary: Tamil Smārta saint of Tiruviśanallūr, remembered with Bodhendra as a founder of the South Indian nāma-bhajana tradition.

name: Lakṣmaṇa Deśika
summary: U31 contribution: author of the Śāradātilaka; details of his life, date and teachers are uncertain.

name: Rāghavabhaṭṭa
summary: U31 contribution: commentator on the Śāradātilaka (Padārthādarśa, 1493/94), whose quotations preserve many lost Āgamas.

name: Mahīdhara
summary: U31 contribution: compiler of the Mantramahodadhi (1589) with its commentary Naukā.

name: Śaṅkara
summary: U31 contribution: tradition ascribes to Śaṅkara the Prapañcasāra, a manual of mantra-śāstra (the ascription is doubted by scholars).
